newsitem.title: UK: Explosion rocks unmanned N.Irish police station.
newsitem.headline: Explosion rocks unmanned N.Irish police station.

text.p: An explosion rocked an unmanned police station near the Irish border on Saturday night in an area where tension is high after a recent surge in IRA guerrilla activity.

A police spokesman said a van was ablaze outside the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) station in the Northern Ireland village of Tempo, some 80 miles (130 km) west of Belfast. No injuries were reported.

British army bomb disposal experts were sent to the scene but police said it was unclear whether the van had contained an explosive device or had been used to launch home-made mortar bombs, a favourite tactic of the IRA.

The incident occurred during a period of heightened tension in the province after a surge in Irish Republican Army guerrilla activities and two recent attacks on Roman Catholics which were widely blamed on pro-British loyalist extremists.

The IRA, complaining that Britain was dragging its feet over the Northern Irish peace process, abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February last year with a bombing campaign in English cities which it extended to Northern Ireland in October.
Security has been tightened across the province to counter a growing guerrilla threat which sparked fears of renewed sectarian warfare between Catholic and Protestant militants.
Britain says the IRA must call a new truce before its Sinn Fein political wing is allowed into struggling multi-party peace which are due to restart in Belfast on Monday.

Northern Ireland's rival Catholic leaders disclosed earlier on Saturday that they had held fresh talks on easing the province's violent political stalemate but did not indicate if any breakthrough was imminent.

John Hume, head of the chief Catholic SDLP party, and Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, signalled they would maintain contacts which are aimed at winning a new guerrilla truce and a place for Sinn Fein in peace talks.

Earlier this week the guerrillas said they would not be deflected from their goal of ending British rule and on Saturday issued a death threat to police informer whose tip-offs which have foiled a series of bombing raids.

The IRA statement was issued the same day that a 27-year-old man was remanded in custody in a Belfast court on a murder conspiracy charge linked to an IRA rocket attack at the city's main law courts last Monday.

Friday's meeting between Hume and Adams was the latest in a series over several months. In December Britain rejected peace feelers arising out of an earlier round of talks which the SDLP leader said would have led to a new IRA ceasefire.

But Britain says an IRA truce called in September 1994 was never meant to last and insists that any new ceasefire will have to be proven to be genuine before Sinn Fein is given a seat in the multi-party talks.
The talks began in June under former U.S. senator George Mitchell. They are aimed at exploring ways of reviving peace hopes but the rival parties involved say the chances of success are slim.
